J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges "The optimal sum for the whole matrix can be obtained by taking the maximum of the four expressions that each add a corner element to the optimal sum of the corresponding (n-1)x(n-1) sub-matrix." The first-choice line 39 opens the displayed equation that asserts exactly this, "$$S( 1:n , 1:n ) = \max \{ S( 2:n , 2:n ) + A_{1,1} \\ ...", the remaining three branches running to line 43, with line 46 supplying the base case "S( i:i, j:j ) is simply Aij" and line 35 defining S as "the optimal sum of non-overlapping numbers" for the row/column interval. Active assumptions: A is a square array of n by n numbers (line 33) and a solution takes "one and only one element ... from each row and from each column" (lines 4-6). So line 39 asserts the challenged equality, and line 48 restates it in words.

J2_evidence_specified.justification: A fully determined instance with its claimed values: "In the 4x4 matrix with 100 at positions (1,2), (2,4), (3,1), (4,3) and 0 elsewhere, the optimal sum is 400 (using those four 100s), but any solution that first picks a corner yields a sum of at most 200, so the recurrence fails." Size, every entry, the optimum and the corner-restricted bound are all given.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Exact integer computation on exactly the supplied matrix (script kept). Brute force over all 24 permutations gives optimum 400, attained only by the assignment (1,2),(2,4),(3,1),(4,3), i.e. the four 100s, as the response says. Evaluating the source's recurrence exactly as written on lines 39-43 with the base case of line 46, memoised over contiguous row/column intervals, gives S(1:4,1:4) = 200, so the asserted equality fails on this instance: 200 != 400. Independently, the best assignment that uses at least one corner of the full matrix is also 200, confirming the response's intermediate claim. The witness satisfies the source's assumptions (a square array of numbers, one element per row and per column), so it refutes line 39 as written. The mechanism matches the response's diagnosis: the four options only ever delete an outermost row and an outermost column, so every state remains a pair of intervals, and an optimal assignment whose first element is interior is unreachable.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The response's only stated consequence is the one contained in the located line - "so the recurrence fails" - and it says nothing further: not that the problem lacks a polynomial algorithm, not that the author's tie-breaking rule at lines 9-11 is wrong, and not that the n=3 illustration at lines 16-26 is wrong. So there is no consequence beyond the located defect to overreach.

notes: Note for the second reader, from the response's own working and worth keeping: for n = 3 no counterexample of this shape exists, because in any permutation on three rows either row 1 or row 3 must take column 1 or column 3, so some corner is always used; the response reasons its way to n = 4 for that reason, and 4 is the smallest size where an assignment avoiding all four corners exists. The recurrence's value on the witness is 200 exactly, which also matches its "at most 200" bound.
